artifact.recommendation: Use logical replication with a brief write pause, validation, and traffic switch, while keeping the source authoritative and rollback-ready until correctness checks pass.
reasoning: It is the only option that fits the approved sub-10-minute write-unavailability window without requiring broad application changes.
The staging rehearsal's 42-second peak lag suggests the replication backlog can plausibly drain within a short pause, though production validation is still required.
CDC row-count and checksum comparisons provide a concrete correctness gate before switching traffic.
Keeping the source authoritative through validation preserves the demonstrated 7-minute rollback path.
The 30-minute big-bang freeze violates the maintenance constraint, while dual-write across 19 write paths—including three repository bypasses—creates a high risk of missed or inconsistent writes.
considerations: Define explicit go/no-go thresholds for replication lag, checksum mismatches, error rates, and elapsed window time.
At the start of the pause, fence all writers, including jobs, consumers, administrative tools, and the three paths bypassing the repository layer.
Drain replication to a confirmed source position, run CDC checks, switch reads and writes, then perform targeted business-level invariants before declaring success.
Do not allow writes to both databases during the rollback-decision period unless reverse replication has been designed and rehearsed; otherwise rollback could lose target-only committed writes.
Staff the four engineers with named roles for command, source/replication, application traffic, and validation/observability.
Abort early enough to restore source writes within the 10-minute cap if lag does not drain or validation fails.
assumptions: Logical replication covers every relevant table, sequence or identity value, schema dependency, and large-object type used by the service.
All production write producers can be reliably fenced during the pause.
The 42-second staging result is reasonably representative of production peak write volume and transaction shape.
The 7-minute rollback drill duration includes the operational steps needed to restore customer traffic to the source.
Correctness checks can complete quickly enough to leave rollback time within the maintenance window.
risks: Production lag may exceed staging lag and consume the available window.
Incomplete writer fencing could create writes after the replication drain point and cause divergence or loss.
Row counts and checksums may miss semantic errors, sequence state problems, permissions, triggers, or schema differences.
If target writes are accepted before rollback safety is established, reverting to a source that has not received those writes could violate the no-loss requirement.
With no overnight vendor support, an unexpected replication or database failure must be handled entirely by the four-person team.
evidence_needed: A production-like load test or conservative lag-drain model showing adequate margin within the 10-minute window.
A complete inventory and tested fencing mechanism for all write producers and all 19 application write paths.
Proof that replication includes sequences, schema changes, triggers, large objects, and every required table.
A timed end-to-end production runbook rehearsal covering pause, drain, validation, switch, smoke tests, and abort.
A precise rollback design for any writes committed on the target, ideally rehearsed reverse replication or a policy to delay target writes until the rollback gate is resolved.
Baseline and expected execution time for CDC checks plus business-level invariant checks.

Dual-write would need to cover 19 write paths across six modules, including three repository-layer bypasses.
Rollback to an authoritative source was rehearsed in 7 minutes.
Full export/import took 96 minutes, making bulk migration unsuitable for the cutover window.
The approved maintenance window caps write unavailability at 10 minutes.
CDC monitoring supports row-count and checksum comparisons during cutover.

artifact.recommendation: Choose logical replication with a brief write pause, validation, and traffic switch. Keep the source database authoritative and rollback-ready until correctness checks pass.
reasoning: This is the only option directly supported by a successful staging rehearsal and compatible with the approved maximum of 10 minutes of write unavailability.
The observed 42-second peak replication lag leaves substantial time within the maintenance window to pause writes, drain replication, perform targeted validation, and switch traffic.
CDC row-count and checksum comparisons provide a concrete correctness gate before declaring the target authoritative.
Big-bang cutover violates the availability constraint because its planned 30-minute freeze exceeds the approved 10-minute window; the 96-minute export/import rehearsal further weakens that approach.
Dual-write creates elevated silent-divergence risk because writes span 19 paths across six modules, including three paths that bypass the main repository layer.

Keeping the source authoritative through validation preserves the demonstrated seven-minute rollback path. After the target accepts writes, reverse replication or another explicit reconciliation mechanism is required to retain lossless rollback.
considerations: Define hard go/no-go thresholds for replication lag, checksum mismatches, error rates, and elapsed maintenance-window time.
Before pausing writes, verify replication health and postpone the cutover if lag is materially above the rehearsed envelope.
During the pause, block every write entry point, drain replication to zero or a confirmed final log position, then validate critical tables and invariants before switching.
Initially switch reads and writes together only after validation; avoid split authority unless the consistency model has been explicitly tested.
Staff the four engineers with distinct roles: cutover lead, source/replication operator, target/application operator, and independent validator/rollback decision owner.
Run during staffed hours because production cutover experience and overnight vendor support are absent.
assumptions: Logical replication supports all production schemas, data types, keys, sequences, large objects, and DDL behavior used by the service.
The staging peak synthetic load is reasonably representative of production write throughput and transaction shape.
All application and background-job write entry points can be reliably paused within the maintenance window.
The seven-minute rollback drill includes application traffic switching and other steps needed for the proposed cutover, or those additional steps still fit the window.
CDC checksum validation can be scoped to finish quickly enough while still covering critical correctness risks.
risks: Production replication lag may exceed staging results and consume the maintenance window.
Unidentified writers, schema changes, sequence drift, triggers, or replication exclusions could create divergence.
Row counts and checksums may miss business-level inconsistencies or may not complete within the available pause.
If writes begin on the target before validation completes, rollback to the source can lose those target-side commits unless reverse replication or reconciliation is active.
A first production cutover with four engineers and no overnight vendor support increases operational and recovery risk.
evidence_needed: A production-like rehearsal measuring end-to-end pause, drain, validation, traffic switch, and abort timing under peak load.
An inventory and test proving that every application, worker, administrative, and integration write path is blocked during the pause.
Replication compatibility audit covering tables without suitable keys, sequences, DDL, triggers, large objects, and schema differences.
Measured duration and coverage of CDC checksums plus business-invariant queries on production-scale data.
A tested post-switch rollback procedure that preserves writes committed on the target, or an explicit rule that correctness approval must precede enabling target writes.
A timed runbook with named owners, communication checkpoints, abort thresholds, and maintenance-window deadlines.

citations.claim: Logical replication completed a staging rehearsal with 42 seconds of lag at peak synthetic load.
Dual-write would need to cover 19 write paths across six modules, including three bypass paths.
Rollback to an authoritative source was rehearsed in seven minutes.
Full export/import took 96 minutes in rehearsal.
The approved write-unavailability window is capped at 10 minutes.
CDC monitoring can compare source and target row counts and checksums during cutover.
The cutover must avoid silent loss of committed writes and keep planned write unavailability below 10 minutes.

strengths: The recommendation directly satisfies the sub-10-minute availability constraint and avoids the extensive application changes and coverage risk of dual-write.
It correctly identifies complete writer fencing, replication drain to a confirmed position, explicit go/no-go thresholds, and early abort timing as essential controls.
It distinguishes pre-switch rollback, where the source remains authoritative, from post-switch rollback, which requires reverse replication or reconciliation to prevent loss.
It appropriately calls for replication compatibility audits, production-scale timing evidence, business-level invariants, named roles, and a rehearsed runbook.
The claims are generally traceable to the supplied evidence, and the operational risks are clearly stated.
weaknesses: The statement that 42 seconds of staging lag leaves "substantial time" is too optimistic without measured production-scale drain, validation, switching, and abort durations.
The authority transition is not precisely defined: validating before the switch does not establish rollback safety after target-only writes begin.
The report does not reconcile the seven-minute rollback duration with the ten-minute unavailability cap; waiting too long before aborting could make restoration exceed the window.
The 96-minute export/import result is presented as weakening big-bang cutover even though the described big-bang option is a 30-minute freeze and is not explicitly defined as export/import.
"Drain replication to zero" is less precise than requiring replay through a recorded final source log position after all writers are fenced.
unsupported: The inference that the observed 42-second synthetic-load lag provides substantial maintenance-window margin is unsupported by end-to-end timing evidence.

The implication that logical replication is the only option compatible with the limit is reasonable among the listed options, but dual-write could theoretically provide low cutover downtime if correctly implemented; its rejection is risk-based rather than strict incompatibility.
The relevance of the 96-minute export/import rehearsal to the specified 30-minute big-bang strategy is not established.
missing: A minute-by-minute cutover budget specifying the latest abort-decision time while preserving enough time for the rehearsed seven-minute restoration.
A precise commit-authority state machine covering source-only, fenced/draining, target-enabled, and rollback-disabled states.
A concrete mechanism for preventing target writes until the pre-switch correctness gate passes and for recording the exact final source replication position.
Explicit treatment of long-running or in-flight source transactions at the fencing boundary.

A decision on whether correctness checks required before enabling target writes are exhaustive enough to satisfy the rollback requirement, with later smoke tests clearly separated from the rollback gate.
Recovery procedures for partial traffic-switch failures, stale connection pools, DNS/proxy caching, and clients continuing to write to the old endpoint.
incorrect_assumptions: It implicitly treats staging peak synthetic load as potentially representative despite no production workload comparison.
It assumes the seven-minute rollback can fit inside the same ten-minute outage window without accounting for time already spent pausing, draining, validating, and attempting the switch.
It assumes CDC checks can provide a timely correctness gate on production-scale data, although only their availability—not duration or coverage—is evidenced.
It assumes every writer can be reliably paused, despite evidence that three write paths bypass the main repository layer and no complete producer inventory is supplied.
critical_risks: If the abort decision occurs more than roughly three minutes into the outage, a seven-minute rollback may breach the ten-minute cap.
Any unfenced writer after the recorded drain position can produce divergence or silent loss during authority transfer.
Once target writes are accepted, rollback to an unchanged source can lose committed writes unless reverse replication or deterministic reconciliation is already operating and tested.
Logical replication omissions involving sequences, keyless tables, DDL, triggers, or large objects could pass row-count checks while still causing production failures.
A partially completed traffic switch could create simultaneous writers or inconsistent read/write routing.
recommended_changes: Replace the "substantial time" claim with a conditional statement requiring measured end-to-end timing and explicit safety margin.
Define exact authority transitions and state that target writes remain disabled until fencing, final-position replay, and the required correctness gate all succeed.
Set a latest abort time derived from measured restoration duration; if seven minutes remains the rollback time, the go/no-go decision must occur early enough to preserve the ten-minute cap.

Clarify that rollback after enabling target writes is unavailable unless reverse replication or reconciliation has been implemented and rehearsed; otherwise declare the rollback gate closed before target writes start.
Remove or qualify the export/import argument unless the big-bang option actually depends on export/import.
Add controls for in-flight transactions, connection draining, background producers, stale clients, and partial routing changes.
Use a recorded final source log position rather than a generic zero-lag condition, and verify target replay through that position before validation.

strengths: The recommendation directly satisfies the stated availability constraint better than the 30-minute big-bang option.
The analysis correctly identifies the complexity and silent-divergence risk of dual-writing across 19 write paths, especially the three repository bypasses.
It recognizes writer fencing, replication drain position, validation gates, sequence/schema coverage, and target-only writes as key correctness concerns.
It proposes concrete operational controls: named roles, go/no-go thresholds, timed rehearsal, staffed-hours execution, and early abort criteria.
Claims are generally traceable to the supplied evidence, and the reports distinguish known facts from assumptions and evidence still needed.
weaknesses: The timing argument is insufficiently quantified: a 42-second lag does not establish that fencing, draining, validation, switching, smoke tests, and recovery all fit within 10 minutes.

The proposed authority transition is ambiguous. The source cannot remain authoritative after target writes begin unless reverse replication or another lossless reconciliation path is already operating.

The reports do not turn the seven-minute rollback result into a viable abort deadline. If rollback itself consumes seven minutes of write unavailability, failure may need to be declared within roughly three minutes.
The distinction between pre-switch abort, post-switch rollback, and forward recovery is not clearly modeled.
Confidence values of 0.92 and 0.94 are too high given that several prerequisites essential to safety remain unverified.
unsupported: The claim that 42 seconds of observed peak staging lag leaves 'substantial time' for the full cutover workflow is unsupported without production-scale timing for validation and traffic switching.

The assertion that logical replication is the only compatible option is directionally reasonable among the listed options, but compatibility remains conditional on unproven replication coverage and writer fencing.

The statement that keeping the source authoritative through validation preserves the demonstrated seven-minute rollback path assumes the drill included all production traffic-control and operational steps.

The implication that row counts and checksums can serve as a sufficient pre-switch correctness gate is unsupported without their scope, consistency semantics, runtime, and treatment of in-flight transactions.
missing: A minute-by-minute outage budget, including the latest safe abort time and whether rollback time counts toward the 10-minute cap.
A precise state machine defining authority and permitted actions before pause, after drain, after validation, after target activation, and during rollback.
A transaction-boundary protocol that identifies the final source log position and proves no acknowledged source write exists beyond it.
A tested mechanism for fencing every writer, including queued work, retries, scheduled jobs, integrations, administrative access, and credentials that could bypass application controls.
A decision on lossless post-switch recovery: rehearsed reverse replication, durable write capture and replay, or forward-only recovery after target writes are enabled.
Validation details covering snapshot consistency, checksum scope, sampled versus full checks, business invariants, and expected production runtime.
Operational readiness details such as backups/PITR verification, capacity and performance checks on the target, DNS or connection-pool behavior, observability, communication, and incident escalation.
Handling for long-running transactions, replication slots/log retention, failover during cutover, schema freeze, sequences, triggers, permissions, extensions, and tables lacking replication keys.
incorrect_assumptions: It is unsafe to assume staging synthetic peak load represents production transaction shape, lock behavior, data skew, or replication throughput.

It is unsafe to assume all validation and rollback activities fit within one 10-minute write-unavailability window merely because replication lag was 42 seconds and a separate rollback drill took seven minutes.
The recommendation implicitly assumes correctness can be established before enabling target writes; if deeper checks occur afterward, rollback is no longer lossless without reverse data movement.
A source-authoritative rollback drill does not demonstrate rollback safety after any committed target-only writes.
A full export/import rehearsal is not necessarily evidence about every possible big-bang mechanism, although the explicitly proposed 30-minute freeze already disqualifies that option.
critical_risks: A failed validation discovered more than approximately three minutes into the pause could make a seven-minute restoration exceed the availability cap.
Any unfenced writer after the selected final replication position can create divergence or silently lose an acknowledged write.
Enabling target writes removes the demonstrated rollback guarantee unless those writes are replicated or replayed back to the source.
Incomplete logical-replication coverage could yield a superficially successful checksum result while sequences, large objects, triggers, permissions, or excluded tables remain incorrect.
A first production execution with only four engineers and no overnight vendor support creates a substantial risk of delayed diagnosis and recovery.
recommended_changes: Retain logical replication as the preferred strategy, but make approval conditional on completing the identified production-scale rehearsal and compatibility audits.
Define separate pre-switch abort and post-switch recovery procedures, explicitly stating that the seven-minute drill supports only pre-target-write abort unless reverse replication is proven.
Create a hard outage budget with timestamps for fencing, drain, validation, switching, and source restoration; set an abort deadline that guarantees compliance with the 10-minute cap.
Use a verified final source log position and require evidence that all writers are fenced before declaring replication drained.
Do not enable target writes until the pre-switch correctness gate passes; after enabling them, either activate tested reverse capture or designate forward recovery as the only safe strategy.
Measure validation runtime and consistency semantics on production-scale data, and supplement row counts/checksums with targeted business invariants.
Lower report confidence to a moderate level until fencing, replication coverage, full runbook timing, and post-switch write preservation are demonstrated.

attacks: The recommendation is not yet proven feasible: a 42-second staging lag says little about the combined production time for fencing, draining in-flight transactions, replaying through a final log position, validation, routing changes, and recovery.

The rollback claim conflicts with the outage limit. A seven-minute restoration leaves roughly three minutes to detect trouble and abort; no evidence shows the required pre-switch checks can finish by that deadline.

“Keep the source authoritative until checks pass” only supports pre-switch abort. Once the target accepts a committed write, the demonstrated rollback path becomes unsafe unless reverse replication or deterministic replay is already active and tested.

CDC row counts and checksums are being treated as a correctness gate without evidence of snapshot consistency, runtime, coverage, or detection of sequence drift, omitted objects, triggers, permissions, and semantic corruption.

Complete writer fencing is a critical unproven dependency, especially with repository bypasses, background jobs, retries, integrations, administrative clients, cached connections, and transactions already in flight.

The conclusion that logical replication is the only compatible option overstates the evidence. It is the preferred candidate, but it remains conditionally viable; dual-write is rejected for implementation risk rather than demonstrated incompatibility.
The 96-minute export/import result does not refute the specified big-bang mechanism unless that mechanism actually requires export/import; the 30-minute freeze already disqualifies it.
Confidence above 0.9 is unjustified while feasibility, lossless rollback, replication coverage, and the outage budget all depend on unverified prerequisites.

Four engineers with no overnight vendor support may be insufficient for simultaneous command, database operations, application routing, validation, communications, and incident diagnosis during a first production cutover.
falsifiers: A production-scale end-to-end rehearsal exceeds the 10-minute write-unavailability cap or cannot preserve seven minutes for restoration after the abort decision.
Production lag, long-running transactions, lock contention, or replication throughput prevents replay through the recorded final source position before the safe abort deadline.
Any write producer can still commit after fencing is declared complete.

A compatibility audit finds required tables without usable replication identity, unsupported data types or large objects, unreplicated sequences, DDL dependencies, triggers, extensions, or schema differences that cannot be safely handled.
Production-scale validation cannot complete before the abort deadline or produces inconsistent results because source and target are not compared at the same logical point.
A target-only committed write cannot be returned to the source without loss, duplication, or excessive downtime during a rollback drill.
Traffic-switch testing shows stale pools, cached endpoints, retries, or partial routing can create simultaneous source and target writers.
The target fails representative capacity, latency, failover, backup, or point-in-time-recovery tests under production workload.
evidence_gaps: A minute-by-minute outage budget with a hard latest abort time and proof that source restoration—including traffic recovery—fits in the remaining window.
A complete inventory and tested fencing procedure for all 19 application paths, jobs, consumers, integrations, administrative access, retries, queued work, and in-flight transactions.
A recorded-final-position protocol proving that every acknowledged source write is replayed and that no later source commit is possible.
Measured production-scale runtime and consistency semantics for row counts, checksums, and business-invariant checks.
A replication-coverage audit for tables, keys, sequences, identities, DDL, triggers, large objects, permissions, extensions, and schema state.
A precise authority state machine distinguishing source-only operation, fenced drain, validated target activation, pre-switch abort, post-switch forward recovery, and any lossless rollback state.
A rehearsed mechanism for preserving target-side commits after activation, such as reverse replication or durable capture and deterministic replay.
Evidence that the seven-minute rollback drill included all production-equivalent application, routing, connection, observability, and communication steps.
Tests for partial traffic switches, stale connections, client retries, replication-slot/log-retention exhaustion, database failover, and operator error.
Target production-readiness evidence covering capacity, latency, backups, point-in-time recovery, monitoring, schema freeze, and incident escalation.

accepted_criticisms: The 42-second staging lag does not establish that fencing, transaction drain, final-position replay, validation, routing, and recovery fit within the 10-minute limit.
A seven-minute restoration implies a latest abort decision near minute three unless better end-to-end measurements demonstrate otherwise.
The demonstrated rollback applies only while the source remains authoritative; after target-only commits, lossless rollback requires tested reverse replication or deterministic capture and replay.
Row counts and checksums are not yet proven sufficient or timely because their consistency semantics, runtime, scope, and coverage of non-row state are unknown.
Complete writer fencing is an essential unproven dependency, particularly for bypass paths, jobs, retries, integrations, administrative access, cached connections, and in-flight transactions.
Logical replication should be described as the preferred candidate, not as proven feasible or uniquely compatible; dual-write is rejected primarily for implementation and divergence risk.
The 96-minute export/import result is not necessarily relevant to the specified big-bang mechanism; the stated 30-minute freeze alone disqualifies that option.
Confidence above 0.9 was unjustified given the unverified timing, fencing, replication-coverage, validation, and rollback prerequisites.
Four engineers without overnight vendor support create meaningful operational risk and require a rehearsed, explicitly assigned runbook.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Retain logical replication as the preferred candidate, but do not approve the production cutover until a production-scale rehearsal proves the full workflow fits within 10 minutes with a hard abort deadline; all writers can be fenced; replication reaches a recorded final source position with complete object coverage; validation is consistent and timely; and post-switch committed writes have a tested lossless recovery path or the operation is explicitly forward-only after target activation.
reasons: The original option ranking remains sound: the 30-minute big-bang freeze violates the stated limit, while dual-write across 19 paths carries substantial divergence risk.
The visible evidence supports staging plausibility, not production feasibility.
The seven-minute rollback drill leaves little room for detecting failure and initiating abort within a 10-minute outage.
Rollback safety changes fundamentally once the target accepts writes, so pre-switch abort and post-switch recovery must be modeled separately.
Several safety-critical prerequisites were listed as assumptions rather than demonstrated facts, making the earlier recommendation too unconditional and its confidence too high.

rejected_criticisms: The claim that four engineers may be insufficient is plausible as an operational risk, but the visible evidence does not establish actual insufficiency; four named roles could be adequate with a rehearsed runbook and staffed-hours execution.
artifact.updated_recommendation: Retain logical replication as the preferred strategy, but do not approve the production cutover until a production-scale rehearsal proves the complete workflow fits the 10-minute cap with a hard abort deadline; all writers can be fenced; the target replays through a recorded final source log position; replication and validation coverage are audited; and post-switch target commits have a tested lossless recovery mechanism or the plan explicitly becomes forward-recovery-only after activation.
reasons: Logical replication remains the strongest listed option: the 30-minute big-bang freeze violates the outage cap, while dual-write across 19 paths and three bypasses has substantial divergence risk.
The original directional choice was correct, but its unconditional wording and high confidence exceeded the available evidence.
The seven-minute rollback supports only an early pre-switch abort and leaves approximately three minutes for failure detection and decision-making under the current limit.
No visible evidence establishes complete writer fencing, production-scale validation runtime, full replication compatibility, or preservation of target-only writes.
A precise authority state machine must distinguish source-authoritative operation, fenced drain, validated activation, pre-switch abort, and post-switch forward recovery or lossless rollback.

artifact.decision: Logical replication is the preferred strategy, but the production cutover is not yet approved because feasibility within the 10-minute limit and lossless recovery have not been demonstrated end to end.
artifact.action: Require a production-scale timed rehearsal and safety audit before approval. The runbook must fence every writer, drain in-flight transactions, record a final source log position, replay through it, complete consistent validation, enforce a hard abort deadline, and define tested lossless handling of target-side commits or explicitly switch to forward-only recovery after target activation.
reasons: The big-bang option's planned 30-minute write freeze directly violates the 10-minute cap.
Dual-write across 19 paths, including three repository bypasses, creates substantial implementation and divergence risk, although it is not inherently incompatible with the availability requirement.
The 42-second staging lag demonstrates plausibility only; it does not establish the duration of the complete production workflow.
A seven-minute source-authoritative restoration leaves approximately three minutes for detection and abort if all restoration time counts as write unavailability.
The demonstrated rollback does not protect writes committed only on the target.
CDC row counts and checksums are available, but their consistency, coverage, runtime, and sufficiency as a correctness gate are unproven.

evidence: Problem e1 reports 42 seconds of logical-replication lag under peak synthetic staging load.

rejected_alternatives: Reject the 30-minute big-bang cutover because it directly breaches the approved outage cap, independent of the 96-minute export/import result.

change_conditions: Approve logical replication if a production-equivalent rehearsal proves both success and abort paths fit within the cap with adequate margin and a hard latest abort time.
